statements.quote: In the pre-test, students were asked to propose innovative strategies to make daily life more convenient within 15 min. On the post-test, students were asked to think of innovative strategies to build an international child-friendly city in Shanghai, also within 15 min. To ensure comparability in theme, difficulty, and structure, the tasks followed established practices in creativity assessment where comparable but non-identical scenarios are utilized.
statements.locator: Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity, pre-test and post-test tasks (saved publisher HTML text; no page numbers)

statements.quote: According to the scoring scales (Ren et al., 2016 ), the fluency score was obtained by calculating the number of non-repetitive responses given by each participant; the originality score was calculated by counting the number of unusual responses (those given by less than 5% of the sample); the elaboration score was calculated by counting the number of responses given by participants that contained specific details; and the flexibility score was the number of different categories from a pre-generated category list used in a participant’s responses.
statements.locator: Methods, Measurements, Cognitive Tests for Creativity, scoring procedure and category-list description (saved publisher HTML text; no page numbers)

statements.quote: Note. This appendix presents the analytic coding manual used to evaluate students’ creativity performance in the open-ended cognitive tests for creativity. Student responses were assessed across four dimensions: fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration, which are commonly adopted in creativity research. All responses were independently coded by two trained raters following the criteria described below.
statements.locator: Appendix B, Table B1, note (saved publisher HTML text; no page numbers)

statements.quote:
The following steps describe how student creativity scores were assigned. First, a structured Excel file was created for each task, in which raters recorded each participant’s ID along with all ideas generated by that participant. Next, raters familiarized themselves with all ideas and performed an initial review, removing responses deemed inappropriate or irrelevant. Finally, two independent raters categorized and evaluated all ideas.
Through multiple rounds of verification and discussion, they determined the total number of categories, assigned each idea to a category, and identified infrequently mentioned (original) ideas.
statements.locator: Appendix B, coding procedure immediately after the Table B1 note (saved publisher HTML text; no page numbers)

notes:
Checked 2026-10-09. Source of record: the complete 76,240-character, 934-line publisher HTML text export in retrieval.json, read in six consecutive chunks including Appendices A-C, references, and end-of-page metadata. pdf_path is null; no local PDF exists, so locators use sections and tables. The saved version is the journal version of record, first online June 8, 2026; the export was retrieved October 5, 2026 and omits figure graphics.

The paper explicitly offers data by email request to the corresponding author. No author was contacted and no access request was made. No c044 repository, registration, analysis-code link, or separate external supplementary-file link is named in the saved article; forms/c044.json has empty data_url and code_url fields. No related public deposit was confirmed in the repository searches. The deposits list is therefore empty: the publisher article and its embedded appendices are not counted as a data deposit, and unrelated search hits are excluded.

For S1, Appendix B describes structured Excel files containing participant IDs and all generated ideas, followed by rater coding and filtering. This establishes that such files were used, not that they are public, nor which columns, arm labels, scores or rows a shareable version contains. No participant data file was available to inspect; row counts, columns, arm assignment, outcome scores and texts in any obtainable dataset remain unconfirmed. Appendix A supplies teaching-activity/scaffolding descriptions; Appendix B supplies a coding manual and a single worked scoring example; Appendix C supplies aggregate Levene tests. They do not supply the complete participant records needed for the requested reanalysis. The generic publisher message 'Data is available for this article' must be read with the explicit on-request statement. The CC BY-NC 4.0 notice applies to the article; no dataset license was confirmed.

what_we_could_compute is null because no usable public data were verified. In particular, final.open_items on exact analyzed total/arm/outcome-specific counts, exclusions and class-adjusted pairwise estimates with standard errors or confidence intervals remain unresolved. Recomputing participant-based arm means, SDs, SEs, pre/post changes and diversity of ideas is not supported by the publicly inspected material. The materials also do not settle test-time AI permission, timing, allocation details or the scoring ambiguities identified by the screening form.

Confidence is medium for the overall public-availability check: the on-request wording is explicit, but current publisher supplementary content was blocked. The main title and first-author searches completed successfully in the four specified APIs; initial Zenodo validation/rate-limit failures are recorded with their successful follow-ups. OSF node-title filtering is not a contributor-name search, so public-user full-name searches were also made. Broad optional OSF surname and Figshare DOI text searches were not exhaustively paginated; their unknown total counts are null. No login, account creation, access request or bot-check bypass was attempted. All network requests used urllib with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1. No remote data file was saved.
